scorecard.calibration: I weighted three primary signals: directional confidence movement across rounds (Bull fell 24 points while Bear held steady at 0.78-0.79, indicating Bear absorbed no damage from rebuttals), rebuttal convergence (four agents independently targeted Bull as their primary disagreement, meaning Bull's arguments drew fire rather than converts), and vocabulary adoption (Bear's 'martingale,' 'Kelly sizing,' and 'naked king' framing were echoed by Macro, Flow, and Historian in later rounds, signaling intellectual gravity). Bear gets the largest share because it set the target number, framing, and rebuttal template that the rest of the panel orbited. Macro and Flow each earn substantial shares because they added genuinely independent arguments—Goldratt's bottleneck logic and dealer gamma mechanics respectively—that reinforced the conclusion through different analytical lenses rather than mere repetition. Historian earns slightly less because, while the dot-com analog was vivid and frequently cited, Bull's rebuttal about reference-class mismatch (defense contracts vs. commodity fiber) partially landed and was never fully answered. Bull receives only 8% because despite losing the debate decisively, the compromise to 15% in round two briefly shifted the Overton window and forced Bear to explicitly argue against the stop-loss mechanism, which sharpened the entire panel's reasoning. These percentages are qualitative estimates of intra-debate rhetorical and logical influence, not predictions about market outcomes or measures of factual accuracy; I normalized by assigning relative weights to the signals above and scaling to 100.
